title: Against Molina: equal grace, unequal outcome is impossible
source_text: CXXXI. Itaque Doctores illi cum Molina dici nolunt ex duobus qui aequali gratia praeventi sunt contingere posse ut unus convertatur, alter non convertatur. Nam qui convertitur, semper majorem gratiam a Deo accepit, quam ille qui non convertitur. Supposita vero in pluribus omni ex parte aequali gratia, vel omnes convertentur, vel nullus convertetur. Ex eorum mente fieri quidem potest, ut in eo qui convertitur non sit, ex parte auxilii divini quo praevenitur, major mentis illustratio, & vehementior voluntatis motio, quam in eo qui non convertitur. Quin admittunt fieri posse ut in eo qui rebellis manet, mens spiritu divino luculentius illustretur, & voluntas fortius & vividius percellatur, quam in eo qui reipsa per gratiam efficacem ad conversionem & fidem adducitur. Sed in eo qui convertitur, qualiscunque divina motio, sive major sive minor, majoris gratiae semper, juxta ipsos, rationem habet, quoniam dispositioni illius qui recipit accommodata, & contemperata est; adeoque ex insigniori benevolentia Dei erga ipsum procedit, & cedit in majorem ejus utilitatem.
pass_a_gloss: CXXXI. Therefore those Doctors will not have it said with Molina that of two who have been prevented by equal grace it can happen that one is converted, the other not converted. For he who is converted, has always received greater grace from God, than he who is not converted. But equal grace in every respect being supposed in several, either all will be converted, or none will be converted. In their mind it can indeed happen, that in him who is converted there is not, on the side of the divine aid by which he is prevented, a greater illumination of the mind, & a more vehement motion of the will, than in him who is not converted. Nay they admit it can happen that in him who remains rebellious, the mind is more clearly illuminated by the divine spirit, & the will more strongly & more vividly struck, than in him who is in fact brought through efficacious grace to conversion & faith. But in him who is converted, whatever the divine motion, whether greater or less, has always, according to them, the character of greater grace, since it is adjusted, & attuned to the disposition of him who receives it; and so it proceeds from a more signal benevolence of God toward him, & turns to his greater advantage.
pass_b_english: Thesis CXXXI. These doctors therefore refuse to say with Molina that of two people forestalled by equal grace, one may be converted and the other not. Whoever is converted has always received more grace from God than the one who is not. Granted grace equal in every respect among several people, either all will be converted or none will.

In their opinion it may well be that, as regards the divine aid that goes before him, the convert has no brighter illumination of mind and no stronger motion of the will than the one who is not converted. They even allow that the mind of someone who stays rebellious may be lit more clearly by the divine Spirit, and his will struck more forcefully and keenly, than in someone actually brought to conversion and faith by efficacious grace. Yet in the convert the divine motion, whether greater or smaller, always counts on their view as greater grace, because it is suited and attuned to the disposition of the one receiving it. It thus springs from a more striking goodwill of God toward him and works to his greater benefit.
